entries.lesson_core_move: Determine whether a continuous-time signal is periodic by verifying that some positive time shift T satisfies x(t+T)=x(t) for every t, connecting the result to later period, angular frequency, and harmonic analysis.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Periodic Continuous-Time Signals
sections.learning_goal: Define a periodic continuous-time signal by the existence of a positive shift $T$ with $x(t+T)=x(t)$ for every $t$, and frame the idea for later fundamental-period and angular-frequency work.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the definition of periodicity for a continuous-time signal: there exists some positive $T$ such that $x(t+T)=x(t)$ for every $t$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with the simplest repeating signal, where one visible cycle matches the next after a positive shift, so the definition can be checked by direct substitution.
paragraph_plan: Open by stating in plain language that a periodic continuous-time signal repeats itself after a positive time shift.
Give the formal condition $x(t+T)=x(t)$ with $T>0$ and emphasize that the condition must hold for every $t$.
Show one simple periodic example and point out how substituting $t+T$ returns the original signal.
Clarify that a signal can have more than one valid positive shift, and that this lesson only needs existence of a shift, not the smallest one.
Close by contrasting periodic and nonperiodic signals and bridging to later lessons on fundamental period and angular frequency.

sections.section_title: Finding a Valid Positive Shift for a Repeating Signal
sections.learning_goal: Read a repeating piecewise signal and identify one positive shift that realigns a full block with the next block.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this section is an example.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text choices; one correct positive-shift value.

sections.section_title: Showing a Signal Is Not Periodic
sections.learning_goal: Show that a signal is not periodic by proving that no positive shift can satisfy $x(t+T)=x(t)$ for every $t$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this section is an example.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable; this section is an example.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed. Keep the example algebraic and avoid introducing a graph when the proof can be made directly from the formula.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text choices; one correct nonperiodicity argument.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a signal with a nonrepeating trend, choose the argument that correctly shows no positive $T$ can make it periodic.
distractor_plan: Use one choice that checks the signal at a single time instead of for every $t$.
Use one choice that confuses oscillation with periodicity.
Use one choice that treats approximate or eventual repetition as exact repetition.
Use one choice that claims a zero or negative shift proves periodicity.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Show that $x(t)=t$ is not periodic by assuming a positive shift $T$ and checking whether $x(t+T)=x(t)$ can hold for every $t$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that a monotone trend changes by a nonzero amount under any positive shift, so no positive period exists.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the failure case for the same definition used throughout the lesson: instead of finding a shift that works, the student proves that no positive shift can work.
solution_step_plan: Assume a positive period $T$ exists.
Substitute into $x(t)=t$ to get $x(t+T)=t+T$.
Compare this with $x(t)=t$ and observe that equality would force $T=0$.
Conclude that no positive $T$ satisfies the periodicity condition.
practice_variation_axes: swap the ramp for a decaying trend
swap the ramp for a signal with a persistent linear drift
vary whether the contradiction comes from an additive or multiplicative mismatch
vary the amount of algebra needed to expose the contradiction

sections.handoff_notes: Use an obviously nonrepeating trend so the contradiction is immediate. Keep the proof focused on the definition, not on graph aesthetics or frequency language.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Fundamental Period
sections.learning_goal: Define the fundamental period $T_0$ as the smallest positive shift that leaves a periodic continuous-time signal unchanged.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image.

question_policy.answer_format: No questions for this tutorial step.
question_policy.practice_question_model: No practice questions; this is direct instruction only.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach that periodicity means a positive repeat shift exists and that the fundamental period is the smallest such shift.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a simplest repeating waveform or sinusoid with one obvious positive repeat shift.
paragraph_plan: State the periodicity test $x(t+T)=x(t)$ and explain that a signal must repeat for every $t$.
Define the fundamental period $T_0$ as the smallest positive shift that works.
Explain that larger multiples of $T_0$ are also periods, but they are not fundamental.
Anchor the idea in one simple repeating sinusoid or waveform so the notation feels concrete.
Close by pointing forward to the use of $T_0$ in later lessons on angular frequency and harmonic structure.

sections.section_title: Checking Whether a Time Shift Is a Period
sections.learning_goal: Check whether a proposed shift is a period by substituting $t+T$ into $x(t)$ and testing whether the result equals $x(t)$ for every $t$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image.

question_policy.answer_format: Five-choice multiple choice asking whether a proposed shift is a period.

Include an option that says the shift works only for some $t$ instead of every $t$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Determine whether $T=2$ is a period of $x(t)=\cos(\pi t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that substituting $t+2$ produces $x(t+2)=x(t)$, so $T=2$ is a valid period.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The tutorial defined periodicity abstractly; this example applies the definition to one proposed shift and requires direct substitution.
solution_step_plan: Substitute $t+2$ into the cosine.
Simplify the shifted angle to show it differs by $2\pi$.
Use periodicity of cosine to rewrite the result as $x(t)$.
State that the candidate shift is a period because the equality holds for every $t$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the sinusoid frequency.
Change the candidate shift to a different positive value.
Vary whether the candidate is valid or invalid while keeping the same substitution test.

sections.section_title: Finding the Smallest Positive Repeating Time Shift
sections.learning_goal: Solve for the smallest positive $T_0$ that returns a sinusoid to itself, using the first full $2\pi$ phase wrap.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the period comes from the sinusoid's formula.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image.

question_policy.answer_format: Five-choice multiple choice asking for the fundamental period value.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Find the fundamental period of $x(t)=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}t\right)$.
distractor_plan: Use the reciprocal of the coefficient as a tempting but incorrect answer.
Use half the period or double the period as numerical distractors.
Include the raw coefficient of $t$ or $2\pi$ without solving.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find the fundamental period of $x(t)=\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}t\right)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Set the phase advance over one cycle equal to $2\pi$ and solve for the smallest positive shift $T_0=4$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This removes the supplied shift and asks for the smallest repeating shift directly from the sinusoid.
solution_step_plan: Read the coefficient multiplying $t$ inside the cosine.
Require one full cycle, meaning a $2\pi$ increase in the angle.
Solve the resulting equation for the smallest positive $T_0$.
State the answer as the fundamental period.
practice_variation_axes: Change the coefficient of $t$ to another rational multiple of $\pi$.
Switch from cosine to sine without changing the period logic.
Add a phase shift that should not affect the period.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the reasoning tied to the first full $2\pi$ return. The example should model how to extract $T_0$ directly from the sinusoid's coefficient, not from trial-and-error shifting.

sections.section_title: Distinguishing a Period from the Fundamental Period

distractor_plan: Offer the true fundamental period as one choice.

example_outline.variation_from_previous: This keeps the same kind of sinusoid but uses a non-smallest valid shift, so the writer must separate any period from the fundamental period.
solution_step_plan: Verify that the proposed shift reproduces the signal.

Compare the candidate shift with the smallest shift.
Classify the candidate as fundamental or merely a larger period.
practice_variation_axes: Use a different integer multiple of the fundamental period.
Change the sinusoid so the smallest period is a different number.
Offer a shift that is valid but not minimal.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the cycle length is stated directly in text.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image.

Subtract to get the cycle length.
Interpret that length as the smallest positive repeating time shift.
State the fundamental period with the correct units.

Use a signal whose repeating interval does not start at $t=0$.
Vary the interval length so the answer comes from subtraction rather than recognition.

entries.lesson_core_move: Identify the fundamental angular frequency omega_0 as the angular rate of one fundamental cycle for a periodic continuous-time signal and use it as the base spacing for harmonic frequencies.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Fundamental Angular Frequency
sections.learning_goal: Define $\omega_0$ as the angular rate of one fundamental cycle and connect it to harmonic spacing.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach that one fundamental cycle corresponds to $2\pi$ radians of phase advance, so the base angular rate of a periodic signal is $\omega_0$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: A signal completes one repeating cycle in time $T_0$; the phase advances by one full turn, $2\pi$, over that cycle.
paragraph_plan: Open by naming $\omega_0$ as the angular frequency attached to one fundamental cycle of a periodic continuous-time signal.
Connect one cycle in time to one full $2\pi$ radian revolution of phase and state the base intuition for why the rate is measured in rad/s.
Introduce the symbolic relationship $\omega_0 = 2\pi / T_0$ as the phase-advance rate for the repeating cycle.
Explain that harmonic frequencies live at integer multiples $k\omega_0$, so $\omega_0$ is the spacing, not just another isolated frequency value.
Close by separating this lesson from later period-conversion work and by keeping the focus on interpreting and using $\omega_0$.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the introduction compact, use the $2\pi$-per-cycle intuition, and do not drift into a full period-conversion lesson.

sections.section_title: Interpreting omega_0 as Angular Rate
sections.learning_goal: Interpret $\omega_0$ as the radian rate accumulated over one repeating cycle.

question_policy.answer_format: Five-choice multiple-choice with one correct symbolic value in rad/s.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given one full cycle duration, ask for $\omega_0$ in rad/s and have the learner interpret it as the phase-advance rate for that cycle.
distractor_plan: Use $T_0$ itself instead of $2\pi / T_0$.
Multiply by $2\pi$ instead of dividing by $2\pi$.
Confuse cycles per second with radians per second.
Choose a harmonic multiple such as $2\omega_0$ instead of the fundamental.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal completes one fundamental cycle every $4$ s. Interpret $\omega_0$ as the angular rate of that cycle and identify its value.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that $\omega_0$ measures how many radians of phase the signal advances per second across one full cycle.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The tutorial stated the definition; this example adds a concrete cycle duration so the learner must interpret the rate rather than only repeat the formula.
solution_step_plan: State that one fundamental cycle corresponds to $2\pi$ radians of phase advance.
Match the given cycle duration $T_0 = 4$ s to the rate description in radians per second.
Substitute into $\omega_0 = 2\pi / T_0$ and simplify to a single exact value.
Restate the result as the angular rate associated with one repeating cycle.
practice_variation_axes: Change the cycle duration to a different rational or decimal value.
Describe the cycle in words rather than giving $T_0$ directly.
Ask for the value in exact $\pi$ form instead of a decimal.
Ask the learner to explain the rate in words after computing it.

sections.handoff_notes: Stay on interpretation first, then compute the value; keep the example symbolic and avoid introducing new visual scaffolding.

sections.section_title: Identifying omega_0 from One Fundamental Cycle
sections.learning_goal: Compute $\omega_0$ from the duration of one fundamental cycle.

question_policy.answer_format: Five-choice multiple-choice with one correct angular-frequency value in rad/s.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a fundamental period, ask for $\omega_0$ exactly using $\omega_0 = 2\pi / T_0$.
distractor_plan: Use the period $T_0$ itself instead of its reciprocal-rate form.
Invert the fraction incorrectly as $T_0 / 2\pi$.
Drop the factor of $2\pi$.
Choose a harmonic multiple instead of the fundamental angular frequency.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal repeats once every $\frac{2}{5}$ s. Find its fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$ exactly.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Convert one fundamental cycle into a period and compute the base angular frequency exactly.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The previous example interpreted the meaning of $\omega_0$; this one requires the learner to extract the numerical value from the cycle duration.
solution_step_plan: Identify the fundamental period $T_0 = \frac{2}{5}$ s from the one-cycle description.
Write the defining relation $\omega_0 = 2\pi / T_0$.
Substitute the given period and simplify the exact fraction.
Check the units and state the result as a radian rate.
practice_variation_axes: Use a decimal period instead of a fraction.
Use a verbal description of one cycle rather than a stated $T_0$.
Ask for the value in exact form and in approximate decimal form.
Vary the period while keeping the same algebraic simplification steps.

sections.handoff_notes: Treat the period as the length of one fundamental cycle, compute the exact radian rate, and keep the algebra minimal and explicit.

sections.section_title: Distinguishing omega_0 from Harmonic Angular Frequencies
sections.learning_goal: Separate $\omega_0$ from its integer-multiple harmonic frequencies.

question_policy.answer_format: Five-choice multiple-choice with one correct classification of $\omega_0$ versus harmonics.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a small set of angular frequencies, ask which value is the fundamental and which values are integer-multiple harmonics.
distractor_plan: Choose the largest frequency as the fundamental instead of the smallest base spacing.
Choose a harmonic multiple such as $2\omega_0$ or $3\omega_0$ as if it were $\omega_0$.
Treat a non-integer multiple as if it were harmonic.
Confuse the count of listed components with the harmonic number.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal has angular frequencies $4$ rad/s, $8$ rad/s, and $12$ rad/s. Which value is $\omega_0$, and which values are harmonics?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use the smallest positive spacing to identify $\omega_0$ and label the larger integer multiples as harmonics.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The previous example found $\omega_0$ from a cycle duration; this one starts from a set of frequencies and asks the learner to distinguish the base from the multiples.
solution_step_plan: Treat the smallest positive frequency as the base spacing.
Check that the other listed frequencies are integer multiples of that spacing.
Label the larger values as harmonics and identify their harmonic numbers.
Restate that $\omega_0$ is the spacing, not the largest or first-listed value.
practice_variation_axes: Shuffle the listed frequencies.
Include one non-harmonic decoy frequency.
Ask for the harmonic number of a specific component.
Give the frequencies as multiples of a hidden base spacing.

sections.handoff_notes: The key discrimination is base frequency versus integer multiple; use the smallest positive spacing as $\omega_0$ and keep the classification explicit.

sections.section_title: Using omega_0 as Harmonic Frequency Spacing
sections.learning_goal: Use $\omega_0$ to generate or identify harmonic frequencies at integer multiples of the base spacing.

question_policy.answer_format: Five-choice multiple-choice with one correct harmonic sequence or harmonic-number identification.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $\omega_0$, ask for the first few positive harmonics or the harmonic number of a specified frequency.
distractor_plan: Divide by the harmonic number instead of multiplying by it.
Skip the base frequency and start the ladder at the second harmonic.
Use uneven spacing instead of equal integer-multiple spacing.
Include a frequency that is not an integer multiple of $\omega_0$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If a periodic signal has $\omega_0 = 3$ rad/s, what are the first four positive harmonic frequencies?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use $\omega_0$ as the spacing to generate the harmonic ladder and identify the $k$th harmonic.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The previous example classified a set of existing frequencies; this one starts from the base spacing and builds the harmonic sequence directly.
solution_step_plan: Write the harmonic rule $\omega_k = k\omega_0$.
Substitute $\omega_0 = 3$ rad/s into the first few positive integer multiples.
List the harmonics in order and verify equal spacing.
If needed, identify the harmonic number associated with a stated frequency.
practice_variation_axes: Change $\omega_0$ to a different value.
Ask for the $k$th harmonic rather than the first four.
Leave one harmonic missing in a list and ask for the gap.
Insert a frequency that is not an integer multiple of $\omega_0$.

sections.handoff_notes: Use $\omega_0$ as the step size that generates the harmonic ladder; do not drift into sums of signals or period-ratio logic.

Rewrite the argument as $8\left(t+\pi/16\right)$ so the phase term disappears.
State that the signal is time advanced by $\pi/16$ seconds and keep the amplitude unchanged.
practice_variation_axes: positive phase sign
phase given as a fraction of $\pi$
same cosine basis with a different angular frequency
answer reported as either a rewritten argument or an advance amount

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example symbolic and one-step-at-a-time: identify $\omega$, divide phase by $\omega$, rewrite the argument, then name the advance.

sections.section_title: Rewriting a Negative Phase Term as a Time Delay
sections.learning_goal: Convert a negative phase term in a sinusoid into a right shift and rewrite the signal as $x(t-\Delta t)$ with the correct delay amount.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the delay is determined from the formula alone.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the conversion symbolic and avoid any diagrammatic support.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices with one correct time-delayed rewrite.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the equivalent time-delayed form of $x(t)=3\sin(4t-\pi/2)$?
distractor_plan: Include one choice that uses the correct magnitude but calls the shift an advance instead of a delay.
Include one choice that leaves the phase in the argument and fails to rewrite the time shift explicitly.
Include one choice that divides the phase by the wrong value, such as the amplitude or the period.
Include one choice that gets the sign right in the argument but uses the wrong delay magnitude.
Include one choice that treats the negative phase as a negative time shift without converting it to a positive delay amount.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable
tutorial_outline.base_case: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Rewrite $x(t)=5\sin(6t-\pi/3)$ as a sine with no explicit phase term and identify the time delay.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that $6t-\pi/3=6\left(t-\pi/18\right)$ so the signal is delayed by $\pi/18$ seconds.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The algebra is the same as the previous example, but the phase is negative so the correct time interpretation flips from advance to delay, and the sine basis replaces cosine.
solution_step_plan: Identify the angular frequency as $\omega=6$ and the phase as $\phi=-\pi/3$.
Compute the delay magnitude $\Delta t=|\phi|/\omega=\pi/18$ seconds.
Rewrite the argument as $6\left(t-\pi/18\right)$ so the explicit phase term disappears.
State that the signal is time delayed by $\pi/18$ seconds and note that the sine basis follows the same rule as cosine.
practice_variation_axes: negative phase sign
sine basis instead of cosine
shift magnitude expressed as a clean fraction of $\pi$
answer reported as a delay or a rewritten argument

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize that the only real change from the prior example is the sign of the phase term, which flips the interpretation from advance to delay.

sections.section_title: Computing Shift Size from Phase and Angular Frequency
sections.learning_goal: Compute the exact time shift from a raw phase value and angular frequency, then report the result in seconds with the correct direction.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the task is an exact symbolic computation.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not introduce a plot or waveform; the learner should compute the shift directly from the coefficients.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices with one correct shift size and direction.
question_policy.practice_question_model: How far and in which direction is $x(t)=4\cos(5t+3)$ shifted relative to $4\cos(5t)$?
distractor_plan: Include one choice that reports the phase value itself as if it were already a time shift in seconds.
Include one choice that divides by the wrong quantity and produces an incorrect shift magnitude.
Include one choice that gets the magnitude right but reverses the direction of the shift.
Include one choice that mixes up radians and seconds and leaves the units inconsistent.
Include one choice that rewrites the signal correctly but labels the interpretation with the wrong time-shift sign.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable
tutorial_outline.base_case: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: How far and in which direction is $x(t)=2\cos(5t+3)$ shifted relative to $2\cos(5t)$?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the phase $3$ radians and angular frequency $5$ rad/s give a time advance of $3/5$ seconds and rewrite the cosine accordingly.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The conceptual rule stays the same, but the phase is now a raw radian value instead of a neat fraction of $\pi$, so the learner must compute the shift numerically.
solution_step_plan: Identify the phase as $\phi=3$ radians and the angular frequency as $\omega=5$ rad/s.
Divide the phase by $\omega$ to get the time advance $\Delta t=3/5$ seconds.
Rewrite the argument as $5\left(t+3/5\right)$ so the phase term disappears.
State that the signal is advanced by $3/5$ seconds and point out that radians divided by radians per second give seconds.
practice_variation_axes: raw radian phase
exact fractional time shift
direction determined from a positive phase
answer stated as a shift amount or a rewritten cosine

sections.handoff_notes: This section should force the learner to compute the shift from numbers, not just recognize a neat $\pi$-based phase identity.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Phase-Caused Shifts in Sine Signals
sections.learning_goal: Apply the same phase-to-shift rule to a sine signal and interpret the result with the correct direction and shift size.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; sine follows the same symbolic shift rule as cosine.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the focus on symbolic interpretation and do not add a graph or diagram.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices with one correct sine shift interpretation.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the time shift of $x(t)=2\sin(5t+1)$?
distractor_plan: Include one choice that assumes sine needs a different conversion rule from cosine.
Include one choice that keeps the correct shift magnitude but flips the direction.
Include one choice that uses the phase itself instead of dividing by the angular frequency.
Include one choice that reports the result in radians instead of seconds.
Include one choice that rewrites the sine correctly but labels the shift as a delay when the phase is positive.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable
tutorial_outline.base_case: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Interpret $x(t)=3\sin(7t-2)$ as a time shift and rewrite it without an explicit phase term.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the same $\phi/\omega$ rule applies to sine and that the signal is delayed by $2/7$ seconds.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The only new wrinkle is the trig basis: the same algebra now applies to $\sin$ rather than $\cos$, so the explanation should emphasize that the conversion depends on the phase term, not the starting shape of the wave.
solution_step_plan: Identify the angular frequency as $\omega=7$ and the phase as $\phi=-2$.
Compute the delay magnitude $\Delta t=2/7$ seconds.
Rewrite the argument as $7\left(t-2/7\right)$ so the explicit phase term disappears.
State that the signal is delayed by $2/7$ seconds and confirm that sine follows the same phase-to-shift rule as cosine.
practice_variation_axes: sine basis
negative raw phase value
exact fractional shift in seconds
answer expressed as a delayed sine or a shift amount

sections.handoff_notes: Make the sine example explicitly reuse the same conversion rule so the learner sees that the basis function changes, but the phase-to-shift logic does not.

entries.lesson_core_move: Classify sinusoidal components in a periodic continuous-time signal as harmonics by expressing each angular frequency as an integer multiple of the fundamental angular frequency.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Harmonics of a Fundamental Frequency
sections.learning_goal: Define a harmonic as a sinusoidal component whose angular frequency equals $n\omega_0$ for a positive integer $n$, and show that the harmonic test is just the ratio $\omega/\omega_0$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the lesson is fully symbolic and depends only on angular-frequency ratios.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. Keep the tutorial and later practice purely algebraic so the learner focuses on the integer-multiple test.

question_policy.answer_format: No questions for the tutorial step; the practice begins in the first example.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the definition of a harmonic as a sinusoidal component with angular frequency $\omega = n\omega_0$, where $n$ is a positive integer, and the corresponding ratio test $\omega/\omega_0$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with the simplest case $\omega = \omega_0$, which is the first harmonic, then extend to $2\omega_0$, $3\omega_0$, and a noninteger ratio that fails the test.
paragraph_plan: Connect the lesson to the earlier idea of fundamental angular frequency as the base spacing for periodic sinusoidal components.
State the rule $\omega_n = n\omega_0$ and explain that the harmonic number is the integer $n$, not the amplitude, phase, or sign of the coefficient.
Work through the base case $\omega_0$ and the next few integer multiples so the pattern is visible.
Show the ratio test $\omega/\omega_0$ and emphasize that only positive integer ratios count as harmonics.
Preview the examples that will test the rule with cluttered single terms, numeric ratios, nonharmonic ratios, and multiple components.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial compact and algebraic. Do not introduce Fourier-series notation, signal plots, or any visual spectrum; the only new idea is the integer-multiple test against $\omega_0$.

sections.section_title: Identifying Integer-Multiple Angular Frequencies
sections.learning_goal: Read the angular frequency from a single sinusoid and classify it as an $n$th harmonic by comparing it to $\omega_0$; treat amplitude and phase as irrelevant.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the worked example and practice can be done from symbolic sinusoid notation alone.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. The task is to recognize the coefficient on $t$ and map it to a harmonic number.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices (A-E) with one correct harmonic classification for a single sinusoid.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What harmonic is the sinusoid $-2\sin(6\omega_0 t+\pi/5)$ when the fundamental angular frequency is $\omega_0$?
distractor_plan: Use the coefficient on $t$ but shift the count by one, such as choosing the fifth or seventh harmonic instead of the sixth.
Let the negative amplitude or phase offset change the harmonic classification.
Confuse the harmonic number with the frequency expression itself and pick $6\omega_0$ instead of $6$.
Claim the sinusoid is not harmonic because the amplitude is negative or the phase is nonzero.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For the periodic signal $x(t)=5\cos(4\omega_0 t-\pi/3)$, identify the angular frequency and state which harmonic the sinusoid is.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the harmonic number comes from the integer factor multiplying $\omega_0$, not from amplitude or phase.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first example to add harmless amplitude and phase clutter; the only new job is to recognize the integer multiple on $t$.
solution_step_plan: Read the angular frequency as $4\omega_0$ from the coefficient of $t$.
Divide by $\omega_0$ to get $4$.
Conclude that the sinusoid is the fourth harmonic.
State explicitly that amplitude and phase do not affect the harmonic number.
practice_variation_axes: Change the amplitude sign or size without changing the harmonic number.
Swap sine and cosine while keeping the same angular frequency.
Change the integer multiple while keeping the same $\omega_0$.
Add a phase offset that should be ignored for classification.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the example focused on reading the coefficient of $t$ and turning it into a harmonic number. The later questions should preserve the same symbolic test and vary only the integer multiple or the clutter around it.

sections.section_title: Finding the Harmonic Number of a Sinusoidal Component
sections.learning_goal: Simplify $\omega/\omega_0$ when the frequencies are given numerically and name the harmonic only when the ratio is an integer.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the harmonic number is determined by simplifying a numeric angular-frequency ratio.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. Keep the example numeric and symbolic so the student practices the ratio simplification directly.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices (A-E) with one correct harmonic number after simplifying a numeric frequency ratio.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A periodic signal has fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0=3\pi$ rad/s and contains the component $2\cos(12\pi t+\pi/8)$. What harmonic is the component?
distractor_plan: Divide in the wrong direction and use $\omega_0/\omega$ instead of $\omega/\omega_0$.
Forget to simplify the numeric ratio before classifying it.
Treat the amplitude or phase as if they changed the harmonic number.
Pick the frequency value itself instead of the harmonic number.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal has fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0=2\pi$ rad/s and contains the component $4\cos(10\pi t+\pi/6)$. Determine the harmonic number of the component.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Convert the given angular frequencies into a ratio, simplify it to an integer, and label the component as that harmonic.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The new wrinkle is that $\omega$ and $\omega_0$ are given numerically, so the student must simplify the ratio before naming the harmonic number.
solution_step_plan: Identify the component angular frequency as $10\pi$ and the fundamental angular frequency as $2\pi$.
Form the ratio $\omega/\omega_0 = 10\pi / 2\pi$ and simplify it.
Recognize the integer ratio $5$ and classify the component as the fifth harmonic.
Ignore amplitude and phase because they do not change the harmonic number.
practice_variation_axes: Change the numeric values while keeping the ratio an integer.
Include a coefficient that requires cancellation before the ratio is obvious.
Keep the same harmonic number but alter amplitude and phase clutter.
Use either sine or cosine without changing the frequency test.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the task focused on ratio simplification. The correct answer should come only after the angular-frequency ratio is reduced to an integer, not before.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Frequencies That Are Not Harmonics
sections.learning_goal: Reject a sinusoidal component as a harmonic when $\omega/\omega_0$ is not a positive integer, even if the ratio is a neat fraction or decimal.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the rejection test depends only on whether the angular-frequency ratio is an integer.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. The main teaching point is that noninteger ratios are not harmonics even when they look simple.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices (A-E) with one correct classification of the component as harmonic or not harmonic.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $\omega_0=4\pi$ rad/s and a component has angular frequency $10\pi$ rad/s, is the component a harmonic of the fundamental frequency?
distractor_plan: Round a noninteger ratio to the nearest integer and call it harmonic.
Accept any rational ratio as a harmonic even when it is not an integer.
Let amplitude or phase determine the classification.
Confuse the fundamental angular frequency with the component frequency.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal has fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0=4\pi$ rad/s and contains the component $3\sin(10\pi t-\pi/4)$. Decide whether the sinusoid is a harmonic.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that a ratio such as $5/2$ is not an integer multiple, so the component is not a harmonic.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The ratio simplifies to a noninteger rational number, so the student must reject harmonic status instead of forcing an integer label.
solution_step_plan: Compute the ratio $10\pi / 4\pi$ and simplify it to $5/2$.
Check whether the ratio is a positive integer.
Conclude that the component is not a harmonic because $5/2$ is not an integer.
Ignore the amplitude and phase, which are irrelevant to the classification.
practice_variation_axes: Use a decimal ratio such as $2.5$ instead of a fraction.
Change the numbers so the noninteger ratio is different but still easy to simplify.
Keep the same nonharmonic ratio while varying amplitude and phase clutter.
Present the component in sine form or cosine form without changing the test.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the rejection explicit. The lesson should make it clear that 'almost an integer' is not enough, and that rational-but-noninteger ratios still fail the harmonic test.

sections.section_title: Classifying Multiple Sinusoidal Components by Harmonic Number
sections.learning_goal: Classify several sinusoidal terms term-by-term by checking whether each angular frequency is an integer multiple of $\omega_0$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the multi-component classification is still fully symbolic and term-by-term.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. The example should stay focused on scanning each sinusoidal term and applying the same ratio test independently.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices (A-E) with one correct classification of all listed sinusoidal components.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For $x(t)=\cos(2\pi t)+2\sin(6\pi t-\pi/3)+4\cos(7\pi t)$ with fundamental angular frequency $2\pi$ rad/s, which classification correctly labels each sinusoid?
distractor_plan: Mislabel one or more terms by an off-by-one harmonic number.
Treat the nonharmonic term as if it were the nearest integer multiple.
Let amplitude or phase affect the classification.
Assume every sinusoidal term in a periodic signal must be harmonic.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For $x(t)=3\cos(2\pi t-\pi/5)+\sin(6\pi t)+4\cos(7\pi t)$ with fundamental angular frequency $2\pi$ rad/s, classify each sinusoidal component by harmonic number or as not a harmonic.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how to scan a multi-term periodic signal, test each angular frequency against $\omega_0$, and label each term independently.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This combines the earlier single-term tests into one signal with multiple components, including a distractor term that is not harmonic.
solution_step_plan: Identify the angular frequency of each sinusoidal term separately.
Divide each angular frequency by $\omega_0=2\pi$.
Label the terms whose ratios are positive integers and reject the term whose ratio is not.
Summarize the full classification without using amplitude or phase as cues.
practice_variation_axes: Reorder the terms in the sum.
Change the amplitudes and phase offsets without changing harmonic status.
Vary the number of sinusoidal terms.
Mix harmonic terms with one nonharmonic term.
Use different integer multiples so the harmonic numbers are not all small.

sections.handoff_notes: This should feel like applying the same ratio test term-by-term. Keep the numbers simple enough that the only real work is classification, not arithmetic.

entries.lesson_core_move: Determine whether a sum of continuous-time periodic signals is periodic and find its repeating period by comparing component periods, angular frequencies, and harmonic relationships.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Sums of Periodic Signals
sections.learning_goal: Introduce the shared-shift test for a sum $x(t)=x_1(t)+x_2(t)$ and show that a positive shift must repeat every component before it can repeat the sum.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the tutorial is fully symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. Keep the introduction text-only and use the same-shift definition rather than a plot.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: Not applicable for the tutorial section.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the minimum effective dose of the periodicity definition: a sum is periodic only if some $T>0$ repeats every component, so the same $T$ repeats the sum.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with two components that already share the same positive period $T$.
paragraph_plan: State the target question: a sum is periodic only when there is a positive shift $T$ that leaves the whole signal unchanged.
Show the base case where each component already repeats after the same $T$.
Use the shared-shift property to explain why the sum repeats when each component repeats.
Introduce the next wrinkle: when component periods differ, the writer must search for a common repeating time rather than reuse the same period automatically.
Bridge to the rest of the lesson by noting that later examples compare periods directly, then angular frequencies and harmonic relationships, and that some sums still fail to share any repeat.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Not applicable for the tutorial section.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Not applicable for the tutorial section.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Not applicable for the tutorial section.

sections.handoff_notes: Write the opening as a definition-first, minimum-effective-dose tutorial. Keep it symbolic, avoid practice, and make the shared shift the only idea that the later examples extend.

sections.section_title: Sums of Signals with the Same Period
sections.learning_goal: Show that adding two periodic signals with the same period leaves the sum periodic with that same period.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the example is purely symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. The worked example should use notation only.

question_policy.answer_format: Five labeled choices A-E with exactly one correct answer.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $x_1(t)=\cos(2\pi t)$ and $x_2(t)=\sin(2\pi t+\pi/3)$, determine whether $x(t)=x_1(t)+x_2(t)$ is periodic and identify one repeating period.
distractor_plan: Use one component period instead of the shared period for the sum.
Add the two periods together instead of preserving the common period.
Treat a phase shift as if it changes the period.
Claim the sum is not periodic because it contains more than one term.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable for the example section.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable for the example section.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Determine whether $x(t)=\cos(2\pi t)+\sin(2\pi t+\pi/3)$ is periodic and, if so, identify a repeating period.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Verify that each component repeats after $T=1$ and conclude that the sum repeats after the same shift.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first worked example, extending the shared-shift definition to a concrete same-period sum.
solution_step_plan: Identify the period of each component from the coefficient of $t$.
Check that both terms repeat after $T=1$.
Substitute $t+1$ into the sum and show that each component returns to its original value.
Conclude that the sum is periodic with repeating period $1$.
practice_variation_axes: Different phase shifts with the same period.
Sine and cosine combinations that still share one period.
Amplitude changes that do not affect periodicity.
Same-period signals stated either by formulas or by an explicit period.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the example strictly symbolic and make the reuse of the same period explicit. Later questions should check whether students can spot the shared period without overcomplicating the phase.

sections.section_title: Finding a Common Period from Component Periods
sections.learning_goal: Find a common repeating time for periodic components by comparing their periods and taking the least shared multiple.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the example is purely symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. The task is period arithmetic only.

question_policy.answer_format: Five labeled choices A-E with exactly one correct answer.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $x_1(t)=\cos(\pi t)$ and $x_2(t)=\sin(2\pi t/3)$, determine whether $x(t)=x_1(t)+x_2(t)$ is periodic and identify one repeating period.
distractor_plan: Use one component period instead of the least common repeating time.
Add the two periods together instead of taking a common multiple.
Choose a smaller value that repeats only one component.
Claim the sum is not periodic because the component periods differ.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable for the example section.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable for the example section.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Determine whether $x(t)=\cos(\pi t)+\sin(2\pi t/3)$ is periodic and, if so, find a repeating period.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Convert each component to its period, find the least common repeating time, and show that $T=6$ repeats both terms.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The components no longer share the same period, so the writer must look for a common multiple instead of reusing the period directly.
solution_step_plan: Read off the period of each component from its coefficient of $t$.
List the first shared repeat time that works for both periods.
Show that $T=6$ returns each component to its starting value.
Conclude that the sum is periodic with repeating period $6$.
State that any larger common multiple also works, but $6$ is the least shared repeat.
practice_variation_axes: One period dividing the other.
Small integer ratios that make the least common period easy to find.
Periods given through sinusoid coefficients rather than stated directly.
Phase shifts that should not affect the period calculation.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the arithmetic visible and explicit. The example should teach that the sum inherits the least common repeat, not an arbitrary period from one component.

sections.section_title: Finding a Common Period from Component Angular Frequencies
sections.learning_goal: Find a common repeating time by recognizing harmonic angular frequencies and matching a shared base frequency.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the example is purely symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. This step should stay frequency-first and text-only.

question_policy.answer_format: Five labeled choices A-E with exactly one correct answer.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $x_1(t)=\cos(4t)$ and $x_2(t)=\sin(6t-\pi/4)$, determine whether $x(t)=x_1(t)+x_2(t)$ is periodic and identify one repeating period.
distractor_plan: Treat the angular frequencies as if they were the periods.
Use the individual component periods instead of the shared harmonic base.
Choose a value that is too large because it repeats both terms but is not the intended least repeat.
Claim there is no shared repeat because the angular frequencies are different.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable for the example section.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable for the example section.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Determine whether $x(t)=\cos(4t)+\sin(6t-\pi/4)$ is periodic and, if so, find a repeating period.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Recognize both angular frequencies as harmonics of $2$ rad/s and use that shared base to conclude that $T=\pi$ repeats the sum.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The repeat is now easiest to see in angular-frequency form, not by comparing period values first.
solution_step_plan: Identify the angular frequency of each component.
Factor both angular frequencies as integer multiples of a common base frequency.
Convert that shared base frequency to its period.
Show that shifting by that period repeats both terms.
Conclude that the sum is periodic with repeating period $\pi$.
practice_variation_axes: Different harmonic bases that are not immediately obvious.
Phase offsets that do not change periodicity.
One angular frequency being an integer multiple of the other.
Giving the frequencies directly so the writer must reason from $\omega$ instead of from $T$.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the math frequency-first. The point is to spot a shared harmonic base and avoid falling back to period arithmetic too early.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Sums with No Shared Repeating Time
sections.learning_goal: Decide that a sum is not periodic when the component periods or angular frequencies do not admit any positive common repeating time.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the example is purely symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. The point is the no-shared-repeat conclusion, which is fully symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five labeled choices A-E with exactly one correct answer.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $x_1(t)=\cos(t)$ and $x_2(t)=\cos(\sqrt{2}t)$, determine whether $x(t)=x_1(t)+x_2(t)$ is periodic.
distractor_plan: Claim the sum is periodic because each component is periodic on its own.
Pick one component period as if it automatically repeats the sum.
Use the sum or difference of the two periods as a fake common repeat.
Infer periodicity from approximate numerical agreement rather than an exact common shift.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable for the example section.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable for the example section.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Determine whether $x(t)=\cos(t)+\cos(\sqrt{2}t)$ is periodic.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the component periods have an irrational ratio, so no positive common repeating time exists and the sum is not periodic.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the negative case: the components are individually periodic, but their repeat times never line up.
solution_step_plan: Compute the period of each component from its angular frequency.
Compare the two periods and note that their ratio is irrational.
Explain that an exact common positive shift would require a shared repeat time for both components.
Conclude that no such shift exists and the sum is not periodic.
practice_variation_axes: Other irrational frequency ratios.
Sine and cosine swaps that should not change the periodicity decision.
Different amplitudes or phase shifts that do not affect the conclusion.
Examples where neither period is an integer multiple of the other.

sections.handoff_notes: End cleanly on the failure case and hand off to the next topic on rational period ratios without proving the general theorem here.

entries.lesson_core_move: Classify a sum of periodic continuous-time signals as periodic or aperiodic by testing whether their fundamental periods have rational ratios and finding the least common period when they do.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Rational Period Ratios and Periodicity
sections.learning_goal: Teach the rule that a sum of periodic continuous-time signals is periodic only when the component fundamental periods share a rational ratio, so the signals repeat together at one positive time shift.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the rule is entirely symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the section text-only and formula-based.

question_policy.answer_format: No questions are generated for the tutorial section.
question_policy.practice_question_model: No practice questions in the tutorial section.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that a sum repeats only when every periodic component returns to the same state at one positive time shift, and convert that requirement into the rational-ratio test on fundamental periods.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with two periodic signals whose periods are $2$ s and $6$ s so the larger period is already a shared repeat time.
paragraph_plan: State that a sum of periodic signals repeats only if all components line up again at one positive shift.
Introduce component fundamental periods $T_1$ and $T_2$, and use the integer-multiple base case to make the shared-repeat idea concrete.
Generalize the base case to rational ratios: if $T_1/T_2=p/q$ in lowest terms, then $qT_1=pT_2$ is a common period.
Explain that the least common period is the smallest positive shared multiple, and note that the same logic extends to any finite sum of periodic components.
Close by stating the failure case: an irrational ratio never lines up exactly, so no finite common period exists.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A sum $x(t)=x_1(t)+x_2(t)$ has component fundamental periods $T_1=2$ s and $T_2=6$ s. Determine whether $x(t)$ is periodic and, if so, find a least common period.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Recognize the integer ratio $6/2=3$, conclude the components are commensurate, and name $6$ s as the least common period.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the simplest rational-ratio case: one period is an exact integer multiple of the other, so the shared repeat time is visible immediately.
solution_step_plan: Read off $T_1=2$ s and $T_2=6$ s.
Check that the ratio is an integer, so the periods are rationally related.
Verify that $6$ s is a common repeat time for both components.
Conclude that the sum is periodic with least common period $6$ s.
practice_variation_axes: Swap which component has the larger period.
Use another integer multiple pair such as $4$ s and $12$ s.
Present the periods through sinusoid coefficients instead of naming $T_1$ and $T_2$.
Ask for periodicity and the least common period.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the example numeric and direct. The writer should make the integer-multiple relationship obvious, then verify that the larger period is the shared repeat time and not just a casual guess.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Bridge from the rational-ratio rule into the least-common-period calculation for a noninteger rational ratio.
tutorial_outline.base_case: No new direct-instruction base case; the example should start from the rule already established.
paragraph_plan: Use a one-sentence bridge, then move directly into the worked example.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A sum $x(t)=x_1(t)+x_2(t)$ has component fundamental periods $T_1=2$ s and $T_2=3$ s. Determine whether $x(t)$ is periodic and, if so, find a least common period.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use the rational ratio $3/2$ to find the smallest shared repeat time $6$ s even though neither period divides the other directly.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Unlike the previous integer-multiple case, neither period is an obvious multiple of the other, so the example must compute a least common period explicitly.
solution_step_plan: Read off the two periods and form their ratio.
Note that the ratio is rational but not an integer.
Find integers $m$ and $n$ such that $mT_1=nT_2$, namely $3\cdot2=2\cdot3$.
Conclude that the sum is periodic with least common period $6$ s.
practice_variation_axes: Use noninteger rational ratios such as $1.5$ s and $2$ s.
Reverse the order of the given periods.
Ask for the least common period after classifying periodicity.
Embed the periods in sinusoid formulas.

sections.handoff_notes: This example should force a real least-common-period computation, not a direct read-off. Keep the numbers simple enough that the student can see why the common period is shared by both components.

sections.section_title: Classifying a Sum with an Irrational Period Ratio
sections.learning_goal: Use an irrational period ratio to conclude that a sum of periodic signals is aperiodic.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the classification is determined symbolically.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the example symbolic and text-based.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic choices with one correct answer; the answer may be a least common period or the classification periodic/aperiodic.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given two periodic signals whose fundamental periods have an irrational ratio, decide whether the sum is periodic or aperiodic.
distractor_plan: Treat a decimal approximation as if it were a rational ratio.
Use one component period as though it were a common period.
Use a rounded common multiple computed from approximate values.
Pick a period value even though the correct answer is aperiodic.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Bridge from the rational-ratio rule into the irrational-ratio failure case.
tutorial_outline.base_case: No new direct-instruction base case; the example should begin from the rational-ratio test already established.
paragraph_plan: Use a one-sentence bridge, then go straight into the worked example.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A sum $x(t)=x_1(t)+x_2(t)$ has component fundamental periods $T_1=2$ s and $T_2=2\sqrt{2}$ s. Determine whether $x(t)$ is periodic.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Recognize that the ratio of the periods is irrational and therefore no positive common period exists.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The ratio is now irrational, so the writer should prove that no common period exists instead of computing one.
solution_step_plan: Compute the ratio $\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2}=\sqrt{2}$.
Note that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.
State that no positive integers $m$ and $n$ satisfy $mT_1=nT_2$.
Conclude that the sum is aperiodic.
practice_variation_axes: Use irrational ratios built from radicals such as $\pi$ and $\sqrt{2}\pi$.
Use a decimal approximation that should still be treated as irrational.
Ask only for the periodic-or-aperiodic classification.
Place the irrationality in either component period.

sections.handoff_notes: The key move here is proof by failure of commensurability. Keep the explanation crisp: compute the ratio, identify it as irrational, and stop there with the aperiodic conclusion.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Bridge from the two-signal cases into the multi-signal least-common-period calculation.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A sum $x(t)=x_1(t)+x_2(t)+x_3(t)$ has component fundamental periods $T_1=2$ s, $T_2=3$ s, and $T_3=4$ s. Determine whether $x(t)$ is periodic and, if so, find a least common period.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Extend the two-signal rational-ratio logic to three components and identify $12$ s as the smallest positive time that repeats all of them together.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This extends the two-signal least-common-period case to three components, so the solution must satisfy all component periods at once.
solution_step_plan: List the three component periods.
Check that the periods are pairwise rationally related.
Find a common repeat time for all three components, namely $12$ s.
Verify that no smaller positive time repeats every component.
practice_variation_axes: Add a third or fourth periodic component.
Use a mix of integer and noninteger rational periods.
Ask for the least common period after confirming periodicity.
Present the periods in a different order or in sinusoid form.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the final example focused on coordination across multiple components. The student should see that the same rational-ratio rule still governs the work, but now every component must fit the same shared repeat time.
